description.narrative:
A Zomba Research and Development Department (ZARDD) response to a cholera outbreak in Malawi, Zomba Diocese through provision of knowledge on cholera prevention and management in three Traditional Authorities of Zomba District (Mwambo, Mtumanje and Nkumbira) and T/As Mposa, Nduwa, Kaugule, Mbiringano, Mkwate, Chiwanga, Mbando, Waiye, Chidothi and Chirambo in Machinga district .
Malawi is affected by cholera annually in isolated areas of the country, which is inclusive of Zomba. These cholera cases have been on an increase since November 2014 with over 2000 patients treated and more than 50 dying from the disease. There has been challenges in collecting information on these cases hence an underestimation due to unavailability of standardised surveillance system in the country. More than 30 per cent of the districts in the country are reported to have been affected with Cholera and at this time the epidemic has spread across all the regions of the country.
The outbreak could probably have risen due to the lack of safe drinking water and inadequacy of sanitation and hygiene. Management of cholera suspects was observed to be substandard by Health workers at both Diocesan as well as Government Health facilities where patients were admitted. Availability of resources to manage the suspected cases has proved a challenge in both Diocesan and Government facilities. Further to this, there has been slow response at District level in sensitisation of communities and alerting the Health workers on prevention and management of cholera respectively.
Cholera is preventable by ensuring access to safe water and appropriate sanitation measures. Death from cholera can be prevented through quick access to standardised treatment regimes in health facilities, something which this project seeks to address in Zomba diocese. The response covers needs in the area of surveillance and response, water and sanitation, infection control, social mobilisation and logistics. Sensitising Health workers in handling cases of cholera and alerting the community on hygiene and sanitation, as well as improving water safety will reduce morbidity and mortality.
This will be achieved through; • Training of Village Health Committees (VHC) • Conducting of door to door awareness campaigns • Sensitising food vendors in markets on hygiene; and production of banners and t-shirts, hygiene film shows and dramas. • Provision of High Test Hypochlorite (HTH) • Production and broadcasting of radio programmes. • Training of 20 Clinicians, 26 Nurses, 16 Lab Technicians, 4 Pharmacy Assistants and 4 Environmental Health Officers in Cholera management • Procurement and provision of protective wear and medical utilities i.e. Chlorine,Gloves, Cannulas, Intravenous fluids • Training of 552 support staff HSA’s and patient attendants in Cholera prevention and hygiene
